pathogen.value: Influenza A virus, with high-path (HPAI) and low-path (LPAI) strains, including subtypes like H5N1

value: contaminated surfaces, manure, egg flats, crates, equipment
on people's clothing, shoes and hands
can survive a long time in cold water
sudden death with no prior signs
drop in egg production or misshapen, soft-shelled eggs
swelling of the eyelids, comb, wattles and legs

LPAI-infected birds often show no signs, or only mild breathing problems

mortality.value: HPAI is defined by killing 75% or more of experimentally infected chickens and can approach 100% mortality on an infected farm; LPAI does not typically kill poultry

diagnosis.value: Signs alone are not enough for LPAI, which needs laboratory testing to confirm; suspected cases in the UK must be reported for official testing

value: strict biosecurity (keeping wild birds and their droppings away from flocks)
cleaning and disinfecting equipment and surfaces
vaccination against specific strains where used

treatment_overview.value: There is no treatment for HPAI; the only way to stop it is to cull all affected and exposed birds. LPAI does not usually kill poultry, so options such as quarantine may be used instead of culling

when_to_call_vet.value: Contact a vet immediately if you suspect bird flu in your flock, even if the signs are mild, since it must be reported by law in the UK.

summary.value: Avian influenza is a highly contagious viral disease of birds that ranges from mild (low pathogenic) to devastating (highly pathogenic, which can kill nearly a whole flock quickly). It spreads through contact with infected birds, droppings and contaminated equipment, has no treatment for the severe form, and is a legally reportable disease that occasionally infects humans and other mammals in close contact with sick birds.
